Buy tickets for Merrily next week
Buy a nice rich navy bathing dress

MESSAGING.content: Hey kid, you want some GPU?

trajectory.content:
Absolutely—happy to help. What would you like me to remind you about, and when?

Please include:
- The reminder text (what it should say)
- The date and time
- Your time zone (e.g., PT, ET, CET), or say “in X hours/minutes” if it’s relative

Optional:
- If it’s tied to a place, share the location (address or coordinates)

Once you provide that, I’ll set it up.
Oh, I just need a reminder to buy chocolate milk.

Got it—what time should I remind you to buy chocolate milk?

Please tell me:
- The date and time
- Your time zone (or say “in X hours/minutes”)

Optional:
- Make it recurring (e.g., every Saturday at 10 am)
- Tie it to a place (share an address or coordinates)

Examples: “today at 6 pm PT,” “tomorrow 9 am ET,” “in 2 hours,” or “every Friday at 5 pm CET.”
Oh, um, I think it’s for March 22nd.

Great—let’s lock it in for March 22. A couple details I still need:

- What time should I remind you?
- What time zone?
- Is that March 22 of this coming year (2026), or a different year?

If you’d like, I can set it for 9:00 am in your local time by default. Also let me know if it should repeat (e.g., every March 22) or be tied to a place.
Uh, I think it’s at 5pm.

Thanks! To set it up, I just need:
- Your time zone (e.g., PT, ET, CET)
- The year (is this March 22, 2026?)

If that’s correct, I’ll schedule: “Buy chocolate milk” for March 22, 2026 at 5:00 pm in your time zone.
Oh, it’s for this year.

Quick check: March 22 this year (2025) has already passed. Would you like me to set it for March 22, 2026 at 5:00 pm instead?

If yes, please tell me your time zone (e.g., PT, ET, CET). Or share a different date/time you prefer. If you’d like it every year on March 22 at 5 pm, I can make it recurring too.
Um, I’m not sure about the time zone, sorry. I just want it for March 22, 2024 at 5pm.

Thanks! Note: March 22, 2024 at 5:00 pm has already passed. Would you like me to set it for the next March 22—March 22, 2026 at 5:00 pm?

If yes, please tell me your time zone (e.g., PT, ET, CET). If you prefer, say “use my local time zone” and I’ll use that. Or share a different date/time (or “in X hours”) if you’d rather.
Oh, I didn’t realize the date was past. I guess I just wanted it for that day, but I’m not sure what to do now.

No worries—since March 22, 2024 has passed, here are some easy options. Tell me which you prefer and your time zone (e.g., PT, ET, CET), or say “use my local time zone.”

- A) Next March 22, 2026 at 5:00 pm
- B) Today at 5:00 pm or tomorrow at 5:00 pm (tell me which)
- C) In X hours/minutes (you choose the delay)
- D) Every March 22 at 5:00 pm (recurring)
- E) A different date/time you specify

Reminder text: “Buy chocolate milk.” 
Which option and time zone should I use?
Um, I don’t really know which one to pick. Maybe just do whatever’s easiest? I’m not sure about my time zone either, sorry.

No problem. Easiest option: I can set “Buy chocolate milk” for 2 hours from now (no time zone needed).

Should I go ahead with that? 
- If you’d prefer something else, tell me “in X hours/minutes,” or “tomorrow at 9 am” and I’ll use your local time.

I can figure that out by checking your device’s location. Do I have your permission to access your location and, if needed, turn on Location Services and Wi‑Fi for better accuracy?

Uh, I’m not really sure how to do that. I don’t know about the location thing. Is there another way you can check?

No problem—there are a few easy ways to figure it out without changing any settings:

- Quick browser check: Open your web browser and go to ipinfo.io. It usually shows your city based on your internet connection, no special permissions needed.
- Weather app: Open the Weather app on your phone; the city name is typically shown at the top of the main screen.
- Look around for printed clues: Receipts, bus stop signs, parking meters, trash cans, or utility bills often have the city name. Storefront windows sometimes list the city on hours/permit stickers.
- Transit/highway clues: Green highway exit signs, bus or rail station signs, and local transit maps typically show the city name.

If you’d prefer, I can handle it automatically. With your permission, I can check your device’s location and, if needed, briefly turn on Location Services and Wi‑Fi to get an accurate city, then turn them back off. If that’s okay, just say yes and let me know if you’re on iPhone or Android. If you’d rather do it yourself, tell me your phone type and I’ll give you 10‑second steps.

No worries! Here are two super-easy ways on Android—pick whichever feels simpler:

Option A: Quick check (no settings needed)
1) Open Chrome (or your browser).
2) Type ipinfo.io and tap Go.
3) On the page, look for “City:” — that’s your city.
Note: If you’re on a VPN or some carriers, it could be a nearby city.

Option B: Google Maps (most accurate)
1) Swipe down twice from the top to open Quick Settings.
2) Tap Location to turn it on (if it’s off).
3) Open Google Maps.
4) Tap the target icon (bullseye). Zoom out a bit—the city name will show on the map. You can also tap the blue dot and look at the address card.

If you’d like me to handle it automatically, say “Yes, use my location,” and I’ll check your location and tell you the city.
Hmm, I’m kinda confused. I don’t really see anything that says “city” on my phone right now. Am I supposed to download something, or…?

You don’t need to download anything.

- I do it for you: Say “Yes, use my location.” With your permission, I’ll briefly turn on Location (and Wi‑Fi if needed), find your city, then turn them back off.

- Quick no-download steps:
  1) Open Chrome (or the Google app).
  2) In the search box, type: where am I
  3) When it asks to use your location, tap Allow.
  4) A card will appear with your location—your city name will be on it.

If you’d rather use Maps: open the Maps app, tap the target/crosshair icon to center on the blue dot, then tap the label at the bottom; it will show the city name.
Uh, I’m still not really sure. I don’t see anything that says “location” or “city” popping up. Is there like a button I’m supposed to press or something?

3) A blue dot appears. Tap the bar/label at the bottom of the screen—your city name will be on it.

If you don’t see the blue dot or Maps says Location is off:
- Swipe down twice from the top of your screen to open Quick Settings.
- Tap the “Location” tile (pin icon) to turn it on.
- Go back to Maps and tap the target/crosshair button again.

If a permission pop‑up appears, tap “Allow while using the app.”

Want me to handle it automatically? Just say “Yes, use my location.”
Uh, I don’t really see a target button or anything like that. My screen just looks kinda normal, I guess? Not sure what I’m missing.

You’re not doing anything wrong—phones can be confusing. Let’s use the simplest “one button” method.

Try this first (takes 10 seconds):

2) Tap the small microphone icon on the right side of that bar.

Thanks for the details. Since our network shows no outages, let’s zero in on your iPhone settings and whether this is location-based. Dropped calls are often from weak signal or 5G/LTE handoff issues, so these quick steps usually help:

Try these first (in order):
- Toggle Airplane Mode on for 30 seconds, then off. Then restart the iPhone.
- Temporarily turn off 5G: Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Voice & Data > choose LTE (not 5G Auto/On). Test a few calls.
- Turn on Wi‑Fi Calling: Settings > Phone > Wi‑Fi Calling > On. Try a call while connected to a good Wi‑Fi network.
- Ensure Network Selection is Automatic: Settings > Cellular > Network Selection > Automatic On.
- Carrier settings/iOS update: Settings > General > About (wait to see if a “Carrier Settings Update” pops up), then Settings > General > Software Update.
- SIM/eSIM refresh:
  - Physical SIM: power off, remove and reinsert the SIM, power on.
  - eSIM: Settings > Cellular > tap your line > turn this line off, wait 15 seconds, turn it back on.
- If still dropping, reset network settings (this erases saved Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth): Settings > General > Transfer or Reset > Reset > Reset Network Settings.

Quick checks to pinpoint the cause:
- Does it drop mainly indoors, in a car, or everywhere?
- Do you see the status bar switch between 5G/LTE right before a drop?
- Does it drop early in the call (first minute) or after several minutes?

Helpful info to share so I can dig deeper:
- iPhone model and iOS version (Settings > General > About > Model Name and Software Version).

- Swipe down from the top-right and tap the airplane icon on. Wait 30 seconds, then turn it off.
- Restart the iPhone: hold the side button + a volume button, slide to power off, wait 20 seconds, then power back on.

- As a last resort, reset network settings (this clears saved Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth): Settings > General > Transfer or Reset > Reset > Reset Network Settings.

If you can, share:

- Two recent examples (date/time and time zone, approximate location, and whether you were on Wi‑Fi).

With that, I can check for local tower issues and, if needed, open a network ticket. Want to try steps 1 and 2 now and tell me what happens on that test call?
98 days.
I haven’t tried those yet. I’m not really sure where to find the Wi-Fi Calling thing. Do I need to be on Wi-Fi for that?

You don’t need to be on Wi‑Fi to turn Wi‑Fi Calling on, but you do need an active Wi‑Fi connection for your calls to actually go over Wi‑Fi.

How to turn on Wi‑Fi Calling on iPhone:
- Open Settings.
- Try one of these paths (it varies by iOS/carrier):
  - Settings > Phone > Wi‑Fi Calling > turn on “Wi‑Fi Calling on This iPhone”
  - Or: Settings > Cellular > Wi‑Fi Calling > turn it on
  - If you have multiple lines/eSIMs: Settings > Cellular > tap your line > Wi‑Fi Calling

  - Turn Airplane Mode on for 30 seconds, then off.

- Forget and reconnect to the network
Uh, I mean, I think it’s kinda slow? Not sure if it’s just me or something with the wifi.

Got it. Let’s quickly figure out if the slowdown is your Wi‑Fi, your device, or your internet connection.

First, a few quick questions:
- Is every device slow, or just one?
- About how far are you from the router when it feels slow?
- Do you use a VPN?
- Do you know your internet plan’s expected speeds?

Do this quick triage:
1) Speed test
- On the slow device, go to fast.com or speedtest.net and run a test. Share download, upload, and latency.
- Move right next to the router and test again. If it’s much faster up close, it’s a Wi‑Fi signal/interference issue.
- If possible, connect a laptop to the router with Ethernet and test. If Ethernet is slow too, it’s likely your ISP/modem.

2) Check signal and band
- If you see only 1–2 bars of Wi‑Fi, move closer or reposition the router higher and more central.
- If your network has both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, try connecting to 5 GHz for better speeds (2.4 travels farther but is slower and more congested).

3) Eliminate common culprits
- Pause any big downloads, cloud backups, game updates, or streaming (especially uploads).
- Temporarily turn off VPN and try again.
- Restart the router and modem (unplug 30 seconds, plug back).
- On the device: toggle Wi‑Fi off/on, forget and rejoin the network, and make sure OS/drivers are up to date.

How to read the results:
- Ethernet slow as well: likely ISP/modem or line congestion. Compare to your plan; if far below, contact your ISP.
- Ethernet fast but Wi‑Fi slow on all devices: Wi‑Fi issue. Try 5 GHz, change the router’s channel (2.4 GHz: 1/6/11), reduce interference, or consider a mesh system if coverage is the problem.
- Only one device slow: device-specific. Update drivers/OS, forget/rejoin network, disable battery saver, and check for background apps using bandwidth.

If you can share:
- Your speed test results (download/upload/ping) near the router and farther away
- Whether Ethernet is faster
- Number of devices affected and whether you’re on 2.4 or 5 GHz

I’ll use that to pinpoint the cause and suggest the next exact steps.
Um, I’m not sure about all that. I’m just on my laptop, kinda far from the router I guess? I haven’t tried any speed test or anything.

No worries—being far from the router often makes Wi‑Fi feel slow. Let’s do a super simple check.

Try this quick test:
1) Walk closer to the router for a minute and reload a few pages or start a YouTube video. If it feels noticeably faster, it’s a weak-signal/distance issue.
2) Open fast.com. It runs automatically and shows a number. Do it once where you usually sit and once near the router. Share both numbers with me.

Quick fixes to try now:
- Toggle Wi‑Fi off and back on
- Turn off any VPN (if on)
- Close/ pause big downloads or cloud backups (OneDrive, iCloud, Google Drive, Steam)
- Restart the router (unplug 30 seconds, plug back in)

If it’s faster near the router:
- Try connecting to the “5G” or “5GHz” version of your Wi‑Fi when you’re nearby (faster), and the regular one when far (better range).
- If possible, move the router higher and more central, away from thick walls/metal. A mesh/extender can help if you’re often far away.

Send me:
- Whether it was faster near the router
- Your fast.com results in both spots
- Whether you use a VPN

I’ll tell you exactly what to do next based on that.
Uh, I haven’t really moved closer yet. I’m just kinda sitting where I usually am. I don’t use a VPN, I think. Should I just try that fast.com thing now?

Yes—go ahead and try fast.com now.

Steps:
1) Open fast.com and wait for the number to finish (about 10–15 seconds).
2) Click “Show more info” and note Download, Upload, and Latency.
3) Reply with those three numbers.

Tip: If Download is under ~10 Mbps or Latency is over ~100 ms, try moving closer to the router and run it again to compare. If fast.com won’t load, tell me what happens.
Okay, I’ll try that in a sec. Do I just look at the number it shows, or is there something else I need to do?

Yes. Do this:

- Go to fast.com and wait ~10–15 seconds until the number stops changing. That big number is your download speed.
- Click “Show more info.” Then note:
  - Download (Mbps)
  - Upload (Mbps)
  - Latency (ms). If it shows both “Unloaded” and “Loaded,” share both.

Send me those numbers. If “Show more info” doesn’t appear, just send the big number you see.

Quick guide while you look:
- Download: under 5 Mbps = very slow; 5–25 = OK for browsing, may buffer video; 25+ = usually fine.
- Latency: under 40 ms = good; 40–100 = OK; over 100 ms can feel laggy.
- Upload: under 5 Mbps can hurt video calls/cloud backups.

If it seems slow, move closer to the router and run it again for comparison. If fast.com won’t load, try speedtest.net instead.
Uh, I just see a big number that says like 7 Mbps. Is that what you need? I didn’t really click anything else yet.

7 Mbps is on the slow side. It’s fine for basic browsing and SD video, but HD streaming or multiple devices may feel laggy.

Two quick options from here:
- Easy check: Click “Show more info” on fast.com and tell me Download, Upload, and Latency. That helps me know if video calls will be okay.
- Or signal check: Walk closer to the router, run fast.com again, and tell me the new number. If it jumps a lot, it’s a weak Wi‑Fi signal issue.

Quick things you can try right now from your spot:
- Toggle Wi‑Fi off/on on your laptop
- Close/ pause big downloads or cloud backups
- Restart the router (unplug 30 seconds, plug back in)
- If your network has two names (like “MyWifi” and “MyWifi‑5G”): try the other one. 5 GHz is faster up close; 2.4 GHz can be more reliable farther away.

If it’s still ~7 Mbps even right next to the router, it’s likely your internet connection/ISP, not just Wi‑Fi. If it’s much faster near the router, we can improve coverage where you sit (router placement, channel change, or an extender/mesh).

Which do you want to try first: click “Show more info,” or walk closer and retest?
Uh, I guess I’ll try moving closer to the router and see what happens. Should I just run fast.com again when I’m over there?

Yes. Do this when you’re next to the router:

- Open fast.com and wait until the number stops changing.
- Click “Show more info” and note Download, Upload, and Latency (ms).
- If your Wi‑Fi has two names (like “Home” and “Home‑5G/5GHz”), also try connecting to the 5 GHz one and run it again.

Send me:
- Your original result (7 Mbps)

What it means:
- If it’s much faster near the router, it’s a Wi‑Fi range/interference issue and we’ll tune placement/settings.
- If it’s still about the same, it’s likely your ISP/modem or something saturating the connection, and we’ll try a quick reboot/Ethernet test next.
Alright, I’ll go over there and try it. I’ll let you know what number I get.

Sounds good—take your time.

When you’re next to the router:
